# Scatter Plots {#ggplot2-scatter-plot}

## Introduction

:::{.callout-note}
## Why this chart

Scatter plots reveal the relationship between two continuous variables: direction, strength and outliers.
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
## Common pitfall

Overplotting hides density; use alpha transparency or jitter when points pile up.
:::

In this chapter, we will: 

- build scatter plots
- modify point
    - color
    - fill
    - alpha
    - shape
    - size
- fit regression line

```{r scat1, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
```

## Basic Plot

As we did in the previous chapter, let us begin by creating a scatter plot with
`geom_point()` to examine the relationship between displacement and miles per
gallon in the mtcars data.

```{r scat2, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg))
```

:::{.callout-tip}
## Try it in your browser
Edit the code below and press **Run**. It executes entirely in your browser
via [WebR](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/) — no R installation needed.
The runtime (~30 MB) downloads once, on this page only.
:::

```{webr-r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")
```

## Jitter

If you want to avoid overplotting, use the `position` argument and supply it
the value `'jitter'`. It adds random noise to a plot and makes the points
easier to read.

```{r scat22, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg), position = 'jitter')
```

Another way to avoid overplotting is to use `geom_jitter()`.

```{r scat3, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_jitter(aes(disp, mpg))
```

## Aesthetics

Now let us modify the appearance of the points. There are two ways:

- specify values
- map them to variables using `aes()`

### Specify Values 

#### Color

To modify the color of the points, use the `color` argument and
supply it a valid color name. In the example below, we change the color of the
points to `'blue'`. Keep in mind that the `color` argument should be outside
`aes()`.

```{r scat6, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg), color = 'blue', position = 'jitter')
```

#### Alpha

We can modify the transparency of the color using the `alpha` argument. It
takes values between `0` and `1`.

```{r scat7, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg), color = 'blue', alpha = 0.4, position = 'jitter')
```

#### Shape

We can modify the shape of the points using the `shape` argument. It
takes values between `0` and `25`.

```{r scat9, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg), shape = 3, position = 'jitter')
```

#### Size

We can modify the size of the points using the `size` argument. It takes
any value greater than `0`.

```{r scat11, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg), size = 3, position = 'jitter')
```

### Map Variables 

So far, we have specified values for color, shape and size. Now let us map
them to variables using `aes()`.

#### Color

You can modify the color of the points by mapping them to a variable using
`aes()`. This examines the relationship between two continuous variables at
different levels of a categorical variable.

```{r scat4, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, color = factor(cyl)), 
             position = 'jitter')
```

We can also map the color to a continuous variable; in this case, you will be
able to examine the relationship between two continuous variables for a range
of values of a third variable.

```{r scat5, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, color = hp), 
             position = 'jitter')
```

#### Shape

Shape can be mapped to categorical variables. In the example below, we use
`factor()` to convert `cyl` to categorical data before mapping shape to it.
ggplot2 throws an error if you map shape to a continuous variable.

```{r scat8, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, shape = factor(cyl)), position = 'jitter')
```

#### Size

Size must always be mapped to continuous variables. In the example below, we
have mapped size to the `hp` variable.

```{r scat10, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, size = hp), color = 'blue', position = 'jitter')
```

If you map size to categorical data, as shown in the example below, ggplot2
throws a warning.

```{r scat10a, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars) +
  geom_point(aes(disp, mpg, size = factor(cyl)), color = 'blue', position = 'jitter')
```

## Regression Line

`geom_smooth()` allows us to fit a regression line to the plot. By default, it
uses the least squares method to fit the line, but you can also use the loess
method. In the example below, we fit a regression line using the least squares
technique by supplying the value `'lm'` to the `method` argument.

```{r aes12a, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point(position = 'jitter') +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE)
```

If set to `TRUE`, the `se` argument adds a confidence interval around the
regression line.

#### Conf. Interval

```{r aes13a, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point(position = 'jitter') +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE)
```

#### Loess Method

In the example below, we use the loess method instead of the default least
squares method to fit the regression line.

```{r aes14a, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point(position = 'jitter') +
  geom_smooth(method = 'loess', formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE)
```

### Intercept & Slope

If you know the intercept and the slope of the line, you can use `geom_abline()`. 
Let us regress `mpg` over `disp` and then use the result to add the line.

```{r aes17a}
lm(mpg ~ disp, data = mtcars)
```

### Add Line

```{r aes17c, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point(position = 'jitter') +
  geom_abline(slope = -0.04122, intercept = 29.59985)
```


## Exercises

1. Color the `disp` vs `mpg` points by cylinders with a plain `Cylinders` title.
2. Add a trend line with `geom_smooth()`: explicit `formula = y ~ x`, no confidence band.
3. Rewrite the plot with a message-first title and `theme_minimal()`.
